text: In 1898, in Kenya, the men building a railway bridge began to vanish... at night.
The bridge over the Tsavo River was led by British engineer John Henry Patterson.
Then the attacks began. Two huge lions, both without manes, crept into camp after dark.
They dragged men from their tents and disappeared into the bush.
The workers built thorn fences and kept fires burning all night.
The lions leaped over the fences... or crawled right through them.
Patterson set traps. He waited in trees, night after night, rifle ready. Nothing.
Terrified, hundreds of workers fled. Work on the bridge stopped.
Even Britain's Prime Minister spoke about the lions in Parliament.
Then, on December 9th, 1898, Patterson waited on a platform in the dark... and fired.
The next morning, the first lion lay dead. It took eight men to carry it.
On December 29th, he tracked down the second lion. He fired nine shots before it fell.
Patterson claimed the lions had killed 135 people.
But in 2009, scientists tested the lions' bones and fur. They had likely eaten about 35 people, though they may have killed more.
For 25 years, their skins lay on Patterson's floor as rugs.
Today, the man-eaters of Tsavo are on display at the Field Museum in Chicago, where you can still look them in the eye.
